overview: The Berar Sultanate was the northern Deccan state ruled by the Imad Shahi dynasty from about 1490 to 1574. Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk turned his Bahmani governorship into independent rule, using Gawilgarh, Ellichpur, Narnala, and the fertile plains below the Satpuras. His successors negotiated with Ahmadnagar, Bijapur, Bidar, Gujarat, Khandesh, Golconda, and Vijayanagara through war, refuge, alliance, and marriage. The last ruler, Burhan Imad Shah, was confined by his minister Tufal Khan; Ahmadnagar conquered Narnala after a long siege and absorbed the kingdom in 1574. Forts, tanks, gates, mosques, a garden pavilion, inscriptions, and fragmentary coin evidence survive more clearly than ordinary homes. Farming, markets, village service, transport, craft, family care, and learned medicine must therefore be reconstructed cautiously. The atlas exact id appears only in the 1492 interval. Its ten-position Polygon contains Ellichpur and three principal forts but excludes Akola, Washim, Wardha, Yavatmal, and Mahur, while reaching northeast across central India to Sagar, Jabalpur, and Shahdol. It begins two years late, disappears seventy-four years early, and is a poor territorial guide.

periods.title: 1490 to 1510: Fathullah turns a governorship into a kingdom
periods.summary: Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk used the breakdown of Bahmani authority to establish independent rule around 1490. He retained cordial ties with some former colleagues, strengthened Gawilgarh and Narnala, and governed from the northern Deccan. The dynasty list places his death and Alauddin's accession in 1510.

periods.title: 1510 to 1529: Alauddin resists pressure from Ahmadnagar
periods.summary: Alauddin Imad Shah sheltered displaced nobles, fought Ahmadnagar, and at times sought help from Gujarat and Khandesh. Berar's armies suffered defeats, yet the state survived among stronger neighbors. His contests over frontier forts show that independence depended on alliances, garrisons, and mobile cavalry rather than an uncontested boundary.

periods.title: 1529 to 1543: Darya inherits rivalry and uses marriage diplomacy
periods.summary: Darya Imad Shah inherited a vulnerable but functioning kingdom in 1529. His daughter Daulat Shah Begam married Husain Nizam Shah of Ahmadnagar, with Karanja and Badnera recorded as dowry towns. Such marriage linked courts and property, but it did not end military rivalry or make the two sultanates one state.

periods.title: 1543 to 1561: Darya balances allies while Ahmadnagar grows
periods.summary: Darya sought alliances, including support from Bijapur, to contain Ahmadnagar. Court histories emphasize commanders, diplomacy, and reversals while saying little about households supporting revenue and armies. He died in 1561. The long reign preserved Imad Shahi sovereignty, but it did not remove the structural advantage of larger neighbors.

periods.title: 1561 to 1563: Burhan rules briefly amid shifting coalitions
periods.summary: Burhan Imad Shah succeeded his father while still young. He resisted pressure from Ahmadnagar and participated in the rapidly changing coalitions of Deccan rulers. The Buldhana history records his refusal to help one former ally and his effort to block Bidar, illustrating how personal grievances shaped interstate strategy.

periods.title: 1563 to 1565: Tufal Khan confines the ruler and governs
periods.summary: The powerful minister Tufal Khan seized Burhan and confined him at Narnala. Authority now divided between a living dynast and a minister exercising power. Berar did not join the four-sultanate coalition at Talikota in 1565, a choice that later chroniclers connected with invasion by Ahmadnagar and Bijapur.

periods.title: 1565 to 1572: invasion, payment, and uneasy survival
periods.summary: Ahmadnagar and Bijapur invaded after Talikota, damaging Berar as far as Ellichpur. Tufal Khan used payment and diplomacy to break their cooperation before the rains. Survival was temporary. Renewed pressure, internal imprisonment, and the strategic importance of Narnala and Gawilgarh prepared the final struggle.

periods.title: 1572 to 1574: Narnala falls and Ahmadnagar annexes Berar
periods.summary: Murtaza Nizam Shah defeated Tufal Khan, pursued him to Narnala, and maintained a siege for more than a year. Batteries breached the defenses in 1574; Narnala fell, Gawilgarh surrendered, and Burhan, Tufal, their relatives, and attendants were taken away. Ahmadnagar then absorbed the Imad Shahi kingdom.

sections.title: Identify the Imad Shahi state and confront its map

items.text: The repository indexes exact id berar as an approximate 1492-1500 state from historical basemaps. Coverage finds one border file, while the missing-card registry retains a Wikipedia-derived summary. No exact card, reviewed override, or staged draft yet distinguishes the Imad Shahi Sultanate from the broader region called Berar.

All fifty border snapshots were decoded. The exact id occurs once in world-1492, with properties from 1492 to 1500 and precision one. It is absent in 1400, disappears in 1500, and remains absent in 1530 and 1600, even though the historical sultanate survived until 1574.

The sole feature is one Polygon, one ring, and ten positions, bounded roughly by 76.092 to 83.620 east and 20.438 to 24.296 north. It contains tested Ellichpur, Gawilgarh, Narnala, and Amravati, but excludes Akola, Washim, Buldhana, Wardha, Yavatmal, Mahur, and Nagpur.

The shape then reaches well beyond a plausible Berar core. Tested Burhanpur, Asirgarh, Betul, Chhindwara, Narmadapuram, Sagar, Jabalpur, and Shahdol fall inside. Direct arcs touch Delhi, Bengal, Gondwana, Rajastan, and Ahmadnagar layers. The polygon is internally valid geometry but historically unreliable territory.

The atlas begins the state about two years after its conventional 1490 foundation, then removes it seventy-four years before the 1574 annexation. At 1500, tested Ellichpur is repainted as generic Islamic states; at 1530 it becomes generic Islamic and Hindu states. Those replacements erase a living polity.

sections.title: Follow rulers, alliances, coercion, and shrinking choices

items.text: Fathullah emerged from Bahmani service and controlled the Gawil division before independence. Around 1490 he stopped treating distant Bidar as effective sovereign authority. His new state rested on forts, officers, revenue, and recognition, not on a clean moment when every village simultaneously learned that a kingdom had changed.

Alauddin faced repeated conflict with Ahmadnagar and sought outside assistance. Refuge offered to displaced nobles could bring useful allies and fresh danger. His reign shows that neighboring courts formed a connected political field where hospitality, sectarian positioning, frontier claims, and military support could rapidly alter one another.

Darya used both alliance and dynastic marriage. His daughter Daulat Shah Begam married Husain Nizam Shah, linking Berar and Ahmadnagar households while towns formed part of the dowry. The marriage created obligations and claims, but later war warns against reading royal kinship as permanent peace.

Burhan inherited in 1561, then his minister Tufal Khan confined him at Narnala and ruled in practice. The imprisoned sultan still mattered as dynastic legitimacy, while the minister directed policy. This divided authority is more accurate than quietly replacing Burhan with Tufal in a simple king list.

The long Narnala siege ended in 1574 after bombardment, breached defenses, and pursuit. Gawilgarh surrendered after Narnala fell. Ahmadnagar captured the ruler, minister, relatives, attendants, and treasure. This was conquest and annexation, not a voluntary union or a harmless change of label on a map.

sections.title: Move among Ellichpur, hill forts, gardens, and work spaces

items.text: Ellichpur was the principal town and dynastic capital, positioned near a route through the Satpura hills toward northern India. Court presence and passing traffic supported its importance. Surviving descriptions are later, so they identify geography and long-term function more securely than the exact plan of an Imad Shahi neighborhood.

Gawilgarh occupied a steep hill setting above Ellichpur and guarded movement through the Satpuras. Fathullah repaired and strengthened inherited defenses rather than creating every wall anew. The fortress could shelter rulers and garrisons, but its present fabric combines multiple periods, repairs, collapses, and later military use.

Narnala covered a large hilltop enclosure with gates, guardrooms, audience space, mosque, stables, reservoirs, arsenal, mint, and other service buildings. These features reveal a garrison community and specialized labor. They do not establish that every listed ruin was built, named, or used identically under the Imad Shahis.

Hauz Katora near Ellichpur placed a multistory octagonal pavilion inside a broad circular pool and garden. Museum scholarship associates it with sixteenth-century design, while exact patronage remains uncertain. It demonstrates elite leisure, engineering, masonry, plaster, and ornament better than it documents the rooms or recreation of ordinary residents.

No excavated Imad Shahi house set provides a standard floor plan for kitchens, sleeping areas, courtyards, workshops, or animal space. Families certainly inhabited town, village, camp, and fort settings, but palace and garrison remains cannot be resized into an ordinary home like ambitious historical doll furniture.

sections.title: Farm, eat, travel, trade, and make useful things

items.text: Berar's plains supported an agrarian state, and most households depended more directly on fields, animals, water, and seasonal work than on court ceremony. Later district evidence emphasizes jowar, wheat, pulses, cotton, and fodder, but it cannot serve as a precise sixteenth-century crop census or daily menu.

Villages clustered around workable water sources and connected to market centers across the plains. Produce, livestock, cloth, tools, salt, and information moved by people and pack animals. The exact volume and ownership of Imad Shahi commerce remain undocumented, so a busy route should not become an invented customs ledger.

Deccan rulers relied on agricultural revenue while merchants and court officers also handled commodities and long-distance exchange. Ellichpur's northern route placed Berar between plateau and north Indian networks. Trade offered opportunity, yet tolls, warfare, monsoon roads, animal losses, and political change could make movement costly and dangerous.

Narnala's stables, arsenal, reported mint, store buildings, cisterns, and gun-foundry remains point to grooms, metalworkers, guards, accountants, carriers, masons, and suppliers. Dating each space is difficult, but the complex usefully restores workers to a fort history otherwise crowded with rulers, sieges, and impressively named gates.

Imad Shahi coinage is exceptionally scarce, and university numismatic research treats legends and types as a limited corpus. Coins can show claims to authority, script, metal, and exchange, but a rare falus cannot reveal everyone's wages, prices, savings, barter, debt, or access to cash across Berar.

sections.title: See households, village service, marriage, mobility, and belief

items.text: Ordinary households joined relatives, dependents, servants, apprentices, and sometimes retainers rather than fitting one universal family form. Evidence for Imad Shahi domestic life is thin. Work, care, inheritance, marriage, worship, and food preparation likely crossed household boundaries, but chronicles rarely name the people performing them.

A later revenue history describes village headmen, accountants, artisans, menials, and servants compensated through land rights or harvest shares, while admitting little detailed evidence for early Muslim management. This suggests institutional continuity cautiously. It cannot assign every Berar village the same officers, payments, castes, or bargaining power.

Daulat Shah Begam is visible because a royal marriage assigned Karanja and Badnera as dowry when she married Husain Nizam Shah. That record reveals property and diplomacy more readily than her preferences, household authority, pregnancies, education, or later relationships. Elite visibility should not stand for all women's experience.

Across Deccan courts, family, friendship, scholarly, mercantile, and patronage networks helped travelers obtain service or escape danger. Berar both sheltered newcomers and sent people outward. Such mobility affected spouses, children, servants, and clients too, although court sources follow ambitious men far more closely than accompanying households.

Fathullah's Narnala inscription invokes Sunni caliphs and Karbala martyrs, while the wider state included communities with different devotional, linguistic, occupational, and local identities. A royal inscription securely identifies its patron's public message. It does not convert every farmer, artisan, soldier, spouse, or child into one religious category.

sections.title: Teach children, train workers, and read several scripts carefully

items.text: The government education history says nothing positive is known about local medieval schooling. No enrollment roll, timetable, teacher list, or gender breakdown survives for Imad Shahi Berar. The responsible conclusion is not that children learned nothing, but that a standardized school system cannot be reconstructed from current evidence.

Children learned speech, worship, household work, farming, herding, market conduct, and craft through relatives and experienced adults. Apprentices practiced with materials, tools, bodies, and repetition. Exact starting ages, lesson order, discipline, and differences by wealth or gender remain unknown for Berar rather than conveniently borrowed from elsewhere.

Persianate court education prized ethical advice, letter-writing, poetry, history, calculation, medicine, and practiced bodily skills. Father-to-son letters show elite pedagogical ideals, not a common curriculum. A polished court secretary and a child learning a first task belonged to the same society but left dramatically unequal records.

Narnala's gate combines Arabic scripture with writing in an Islamicate monumental tradition, while administration operated among Persian, Marathi, and other spoken languages. Surviving inscriptions prove specialist readers, composers, calligraphers, and stonecutters. They do not prove that most residents read the script or spoke the language carved above them.

Learning at a fort also included watch routines, animal care, weapons maintenance, storage, water management, signaling, and navigation. These skills rarely appear as a syllabus. Narnala's many functional spaces make practical training plausible, although the ruins do not preserve who taught whom or who occasionally dropped the keys.

sections.title: Treat illness, injury, diet, and care without inventing a hospital

items.text: Deccan learned medicine joined Islamicate Unani traditions with knowledge drawn from Indic drugs, treatments, diet, climate, and surgery. Physicians compared texts and local practice. This regional evidence makes plural medicine plausible in Berar, but no reviewed source identifies a resident Imad Shahi court physician or a standard treatment followed by everyone.

Humoral reasoning linked health with seasons, foods, smells, environment, and bodily balance. Deccan writers discussed local fruits and remedies for newcomers. Such advice represents learned practice, not every household's explanation of sickness. Patients could also rely on family knowledge, religious care, herbal experience, or practitioners absent from court texts.

Campaigns and sieges brought wounds, infection, hunger, exhaustion, displacement, and grief to soldiers and civilians. The final Narnala siege involved prolonged bombardment and assault. Chronicles celebrate strategy more readily than nursing, disability, burial, or recovery, leaving the people who carried water and dressed injuries mostly unnamed.

Families and companions were the nearest likely caregivers for many illnesses, but the exact division of care by age, gender, occupation, or status is not recorded. Water, food, rest, fuel, transport, remedies, and shelter shaped survival. A plausible care setting is still not a documented patient case.

No reviewed source documents an Imad Shahi hospital, dispensary, pharmacy, medical school, patient register, or public-health office in Berar. Neighboring Deccan courts had learned physicians and institutions, but importing their buildings would create false certainty. The card therefore records regional medical context and a specific local absence.

sections.title: Store water, move overflow, and bound claims about waste

items.text: Narnala reportedly held twenty-two tanks, six retaining water throughout the year. Reservoirs supported drinking, cooking, animals, worship, building, firefighting, and siege endurance. Counts come from a layered fort description, so not every basin can be assigned to one Imad Shahi reign or assumed equally clean and accessible.

Stone drains conveyed surface water into cisterns and moved overflow from one basin to another. That network is practical hydraulic engineering shaped by hilltop scarcity. It reduced wasted rainfall, yet drains and storage required clearing and repair; a beautifully planned channel could still clog at the least convenient monsoon moment.

Four covered cisterns stood near Narnala's mosque and stables. Local tradition associated them with storing oil and ghee for the garrison, while some observers proposed water storage. The conflicting interpretations should remain visible. Covered masonry proves storage capacity more securely than the identity of every liquid once inside.

Hauz Katora made stored water part of elite landscape and leisure through a pavilion rising within a circular pool. Deccan waterworks also expressed patronage and political power. This does not mean ordinary homes enjoyed fountains, private baths, or reliable supply; later records repeatedly show how water constrained settlement and cultivation.

Reviewed sources do not document a standard Imad Shahi toilet, household latrine, sewer, refuse service, street-cleaning schedule, or method for disposing of human waste and animal dung. These materials required handling, but specific sanitation routines remain unknown. Tanks and drains alone are not permission to invent a citywide sewer system.

sections.title: Recognize forts, architecture, epigraphy, and secure writing

items.text: Strengthening Gawilgarh and Narnala joined topography, masonry, gates, reservoirs, storage, stables, and garrison labor into a northern defense system. The achievement was collective and layered: surveyors, quarry workers, masons, carriers, carpenters, metalworkers, water managers, soldiers, and earlier builders all contributed to structures later rulers kept changing.

The ornate Mahakali Gate at Narnala bears inscriptions dated AH 892, equivalent to 1487, naming Fathullah before independence while Mahmud Shah Bahmani still reigned. The gate makes political transition visible in stone: a provincial commander advertised piety, patronage, and authority several years before founding his own sultanate.

Secure writing sample: original Arabic in Arabic script, “وَمَن دَخَلَهُ كَانَ آمِنًا”; transliteration “wa-man dakhalahu kana aminan”; translation “Whoever enters it shall be safe.” Quran 3:97 is quoted on Narnala's upper Mahakali Gate inscription of 1487, patronized by Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk and signed by writer Muhammad Abdullah.

Hauz Katora's octagonal tower, pool, galleries, stucco, screens, niches, and rosette bosses show sophisticated leisure architecture around Ellichpur. Attribution remains cautious because the monument lacks a surviving dedicatory inscription and may bridge Imad Shahi and Nizam Shahi practice. Uncertainty belongs in the achievement, not behind it.

Little securely attributable portable art survives from Berar, and museum scholarship notes that the state left a much thinner material record than neighboring courts. Scarcity is a finding, not proof of cultural emptiness. Perishable textiles, wood, food, music, and daily tools rarely survive as loyally as stone gates.

sections.title: End sovereignty in 1574 and follow people beyond it

items.text: Ahmadnagar's forces captured Narnala in 1574 after sustained batteries and assault; Gawilgarh then surrendered. Burhan Imad Shah and Tufal Khan were taken with relatives and attendants. The annexation ended independent Imad Shahi institutions, diplomacy, and succession, even though administrative practice could be reused under new authority.

A district history reports that Burhan, Tufal, Shamshir-ul-Mulk, their families, and followers were sent to an Ahmadnagar fortress and soon died. The account's explanation is uncertain, but captivity is clear. Ending a kingdom could be a household catastrophe, not merely a tidy arrow between colored polygons.

Farmers, herders, traders, artisans, worshippers, children, healers, and water workers remained after conquest. They negotiated new officials, demands, opportunities, and dangers while maintaining some fields, routes, skills, relationships, and places. Political continuity ended in 1574; social and material continuities crossed that date unevenly rather than freezing.

The Imad Shahi Sultanate must stay separate from the Bahmani province before 1490, Ahmadnagar after 1574, the Mughal subah, Maratha administrations, Hyderabad's later province, and British Berar. Shared land and reused forts document succession. They do not authorize one card or one continuous state identity across centuries.

The atlas exact id vanishes at 1500 while the dynasty has seventy-four years left. Later layers assign Ellichpur to generic Islamic states and then generic Islamic and Hindu states, while Ahmadnagar already occupies several tested Berar locations in 1492. The card corrects the lifetime without endorsing the distorted polygon.

ending.text: In 1574, after more than a year of siege operations, Ahmadnagar's forces breached and captured Narnala; Gawilgarh surrendered soon afterward. Burhan Imad Shah, the minister Tufal Khan, relatives, attendants, and commanders were taken into custody, and the Imad Shahi Sultanate was absorbed into the Nizam Shahi state. This ended Berar's independent dynasty, diplomacy, and succession, but it did not empty Ellichpur, the plains, villages, forts, markets, gardens, or waterworks. Families continued farming, trading, worshipping, learning, making, healing, and caring under changed authority. The atlas creates the opposite error: it removes exact id berar at 1500, seventy-four years before annexation, and uses broad generic layers afterward. The historical card therefore runs from circa 1490 to 1574 and records no automated predecessor or successor association. The Bahmani province, Ahmadnagar kingdom, Mughal subah, Maratha governments, Hyderabad province, and British Berar remain distinct identities despite territorial overlap and reused institutions.
